newsitem.title: BURMA: Burma's Suu Kyi dismisses restrictions as "silly".
newsitem.headline: Burma's Suu Kyi dismisses restrictions as "silly".

text.p: A top Burmese official said on Thursday restrictions would remain on democracy leader Aung San Suu Kyi for her own safety, a statement dismissed by the Nobel Peace laureate as "very silly".

Senior intelligence official Colonel Thein Swe told Reuters the decision made in early December following student unrest to require Suu Kyi to inform the government of her movements and visitors was made to protect, not inconvenience, her.

"We are concerned for her. We are responsible for her safety, and if something happens to her we have to take the blame," Thein Swe said after the monthly news briefing of the ruling State Law and Order Restoration Council (SLORC).
He told the news conference he did not know when the restrictions might be lifted, saying only it would be when the situation normalised.

But Suu Kyi, who was released from six years of house arrest in July 1995, told Reuters in a telephone interview on Thursday it was "very silly" to presume the restrictions were imposed for her benefit.
"That's a very silly thing to say. I don't take them seriously and hope you don't either," she said. "I don't think they are helping me in any way."

Suu Kyi has to advise officials of her social plans, and they make arrangements for her to travel to places within Rangoon or allow visitors past the blockades blocking traffic from entering her street.

SLORC officials in early December placed restrictions on Suu Kyi following a wave a protests, when several thousand students took to the street in rare demonstrations against the military authorities.
The government has accused Suu Kyi's National League for Democracy (NLD) party of politicising the student protests. NLD officials and the students have denied any collaboration between the groups.

Another senior intelligence official, Colonel Kyaw Thein, told reporters there could be some links between the student unrest and the December 25 incident when two time bombs exploded at a Buddhist site in a Rangoon suburb, killing five people and wounding 17.
He said he could not rule out the possibility the NLD could be involved to some extent in the bombing.

"I don't deny (the possibility). There are a lot of possibilities," he said after the briefing. "I don't know exactly who are the responsible persons who placed the bomb and who directed them. We don't have the evidence yet."

The government has blamed an ethnic guerrilla organisation -- the Karen National Union (KNU) -- and exiled dissidents for the bombings. The KNU and the Thai-based dissident students group have denied involvement.
Separately, Suu Kyi told Reuters the NLD planned to continue its efforts to bring democracy to Burma in the coming year.
"In one word, what I want for this year is democracy," she said, repeating a request for increased pressure by the international community to help reach the goal.
"I think the international community should do everything it can to help in the fight for democracy," she said.
